This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic value of miR-193b-5p and miR-511-5p in sepsis and septic shock from the perspective of immune regulation. Initially, serum exosomal miRNA sequencing was conducted on patients with sepsis ( n = 6), septic shock ( n = 6), and healthy controls ( n = 3). Using bioinformatics analysis, miR-193b-5p and miR-511-5p were identified as immune-related miRNAs differentiating sepsis from septic shock. Subsequently, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) was performed to validate the identified miRNAs in a cohort of 90 participants, including 30 patients with sepsis, 30 with septic shock, and 30 general surgery patients serving as controls. The results indicated that miR-193b-5p expression level was significantly reduced in septic patients and septic shock patients compared with healthy controls. Both miR-193b-5p and miR-511-5p exhibited diagnostic potential, distinguishing sepsis from the control group, with area under the curve values of 0.797 and 0.795, respectively ( P < 0.05). Furthermore, miR-193b-5p expression level was inversely correlated with C-reactive protein level ( r = -0.40, P < 0.001), procalcitonin level ( r = -0.31, P = 0.003), and interleukin-6 level ( r = -0.39, P < 0.001). A positive correlation was identified between miR-193b-5p and lymphocyte count ( r = 0.26, P = 0.014). In conclusion, serum miR-193b-5p demonstrated potential as a diagnostic biomarker for sepsis and was associated with inflammation and immune regulation in sepsis. Keywords Sepsis Septic shock MicroRNAs Biomarker Immune regulation Subject terms Bioinformatics High-throughput screening Transcriptomics Sepsis Diagnostic markers Ningxia Natural Science Foundation Project 2022A1782 https://doi.org/10.13039/100016692 Key Research and Development Program of Ningxia 2021BEG03064 issue-copyright-statement © Springer Nature Limited 2025 Introduction Sepsis was defined as “life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection” by the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis 3.0), and it is one of the most life-threatening critical infectious diseases. Septic shock is a subset of sepsis where particularly profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities substantially increase mortality 1 . There are approximately 48.9 million septic patients, and 11 million septic patients die worldwide annually, accounting for 19.7% of all the global deaths 2 . The morbidity and mortality rates of sepsis are extremely high, causing a huge financial burden and consumption of medical resources on countries around the world, as well as imposing heavy burden to families. The 2021 international guidelines for the management of sepsis and septic shock emphasize that early recognition and timely, appropriate treatment of these conditions can significantly reduce morbidity and mortality. Additionally, such measures improve both short- and long-term patient prognoses, decrease hospital stay, and alleviate the economic burden on individuals and the healthcare system 3 . However, at present, blood cultures and inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), interleukin (IL)-6, and white blood cell (WBC) count, fail to diagnose sepsis with sufficient speed and accuracy. According to the Sepsis 3.0 criteria, further investigation into the pathogenesis of sepsis and the identification of highly specific and sensitive biomarkers are necessary to establish a robust theoretical basis for clinical diagnosis and treatment. Sepsis is characterized by a complex pathophysiology involving pro-inflammatory responses, immune suppression, and endothelial dysfunction. The immune inflammatory response plays a pivotal role in the development of sepsis 4 . In the early stages of the disease, various immune cells and their released inflammatory mediators and cytokines can trigger an exaggerated inflammatory response. Conversely, the later stages are marked by prolonged and severe immunosuppression. The immune-mediated damage, contributing to organ dysfunction, is regulated by a complex molecular network throughout the body. Investigating the role of the immune response in the development and progression of sepsis, identifying key regulatory points, and implementing interventions at these points can significantly improve the effectiveness of sepsis management in clinical practice 5 . Over the past fifteen years, microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as promising biomarkers due to their sensitivity, specificity, and accessibility 6 . Meanwhile, miRNAs play a central role in sepsis pathogenesis 7 . MiRNAs are endogenous non-coding RNA molecules of approximately 21 nucleotides in length. They do not encode proteins, whereas regulate their expression by binding to target genes. Partial binding to the target gene can inhibit their expression, while complete binding can lead to the loss of function. MiRNAs account for only 1% of the human genome, while regulate up to 60% of genes and play a pivotal role in regulating gene expression networks 8 . They play critical roles in a wide range of cellular and organismal functions 9 , they have been identified as potential biomarkers for numerous diseases and viable targets for therapeutic interventions 10 . Although some miRNAs have exhibited to be associated with the development of sepsis 11 , sepsis is a heterogeneous, dynamic syndrome caused by imbalance in the inflammatory network. However, a single indicator or a small set of indicators is insufficient to comprehensively reflect the dysregulation of immune and inflammatory responses in sepsis. The present study therefore utilized high-throughput sequencing technology to obtain all miRNAs in serum exosomes from patients with sepsis and septic shock, and potential biomarkers were screened and verified for the early sepsis diagnosis from the perspective of immune function.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: sepsis and septic shock progression and severity, compared to healthy controls
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Significantly reduced (downregulated) in septic and septic shock patients compared to healthy controls, but no significant difference was observed between sepsis and septic shock stages. Levels are inversely correlated with inflammatory markers (PCT, CRP, IL-6) and positively correlated with lymphocyte count (LYC).
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Demonstrated diagnostic potential for distinguishing sepsis from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.797 (P < 0.05), sensitivity 85.0%, and specificity 73.3% (optimal cutoff 2.08). It acts as a protective factor (OR=0.267, 95% CI: 0.081–0.877). Levels are inversely correlated with C-reactive protein (r = -0.40, P < 0.001), procalcitonin (r = -0.31, P = 0.003), and interleukin-6 (r = -0.39, P < 0.001), and positively correlated with lymphocyte count (r = 0.26, P = 0.014). Lower levels (≤ 2.08) are associated with more severe inflammatory responses and reduced lymphocyte count. No significant diagnostic utility (AUC=0.587) for distinguishing sepsis from septic shock.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Sepsis and Septic Shock pathogenesis, progression, and immune function regulation, including inflammatory responses.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are endogenous non-coding RNA molecules that regulate gene expression by binding to target genes, inhibiting their expression or leading to loss of function. Despite accounting for only 1% of the human genome, they regulate up to 60% of genes and play a pivotal role in gene expression networks. The study identified miR-193b-5p and miR-511-5p as immune-related miRNAs, with miR-193b-5p specifically associated with inflammation and immune regulation in sepsis. Molecular mechanisms involve the dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses, such as leukocyte transendothelial migration and T cell receptor (TCR) signaling pathways, which are critical in sepsis pathogenesis and progression. Downregulated target genes between sepsis and septic shock were enriched in leukocyte transendothelial migration and TCR signaling. Upregulated target genes between septic patients and healthy controls were enriched in Fc epsilon RI signaling, Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis, and TCR signaling. For septic shock patients versus healthy controls, upregulated target genes were primarily involved in T helper (Th) 17 cell differentiation, TCR signaling, Fc epsilon RI signaling, leukocyte transendothelial migration, IL-17 signaling, Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation, and NOD-like receptor signaling pathways. miR-193b-5p is linked to target genes like NFATC2, MAP2K7, and CLDN2. MAP2K7, a hub gene, is involved in proinflammatory cytokine responses and enriched in the TCR signaling pathway. Upregulation of the TCR signaling pathway in septic shock compared to sepsis suggests early immune overactivation, potentially driving the transition to septic shock. The overall molecular mechanism exploration involved bioinformatics analysis using multiple databases to identify miRNA-mRNA interaction pairs, hub genes, and key differentially expressed miRNAs (DEMs) related to immune function pathways.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Severity-dependent differential expression of miRNAs was observed. miR-193b-5p expression was significantly reduced in both septic patients and septic shock patients compared to healthy controls, with lower levels (≤ 2.08) correlating with more severe inflammatory responses, clinical symptoms, and reduced lymphocyte count, indicating a correlation with disease severity. However, no significant difference in miR-193b-5p levels was found between sepsis and septic shock stages. miR-511-5p did not show significant differences across healthy controls, sepsis, and septic shock groups. The septic shock group consistently showed higher severity markers like APACHE II scores and maximum body temperatures compared to sepsis and control groups. Different numbers of differentially expressed miRNAs (DEMs) were found when comparing sepsis vs HCs (124 DEMs), septic shock vs HCs (212 DEMs), and sepsis vs septic shock (19 DEMs), suggesting a stronger effect with increased disease severity when compared to HCs. The TCR signaling pathway was notably upregulated in the septic shock group compared with the sepsis group.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: miR-193b-5p exhibited good diagnostic potential for distinguishing sepsis patients from healthy controls, with an AUC of 0.797 (sensitivity 85.0%, specificity 73.3%) at an optimal cutoff of 2.08. Initial findings suggested miR-511-5p also had diagnostic potential for sepsis from controls (AUC 0.795), but further analysis indicated no significant difference in its expression between disease groups and healthy controls, showing limited utility. Neither miR-193b-5p nor miR-511-5p, nor their combination, demonstrated high specificity or significant predictive performance for differentiating sepsis from septic shock stages (AUCs ~0.5), indicating low specificity for distinguishing between these two disease severities.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Adult patients (≥ 18 years old) with sepsis, septic shock, healthy controls, and general surgery patients as control groups. The study cohorts included an initial sequencing group and a larger validation cohort.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Serum miR-193b-5p demonstrated significant potential as a diagnostic biomarker for sepsis, capable of distinguishing septic patients from healthy controls and correlating with sepsis severity (e.g., SOFA score, inflammatory markers). Its early recognition and timely diagnosis could significantly reduce morbidity and mortality, improve patient prognoses, decrease hospital stay, and alleviate economic burdens associated with sepsis and septic shock. The findings highlight the critical role of inflammation and immune regulation in sepsis pathophysiology and provide a theoretical basis for accurate diagnosis and targeted treatment, particularly given that lower miR-193b-5p levels are associated with more severe inflammatory responses and clinical symptoms.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: miR-193b-5p holds diagnostic utility for sepsis and for assessing its severity, acting as a potential protective factor against sepsis and septic shock progression. Lower levels of miR-193b-5p are associated with increased adverse risk, indicated by more severe inflammatory responses and clinical symptoms.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: MiRNAs generally show promise as biomarkers due to their sensitivity, specificity, and accessibility. miR-193b-5p demonstrated good reliability and predictive ability for distinguishing septic patients from healthy controls (AUC 0.797, sensitivity 85.0%, specificity 73.3%) and significant correlations with inflammation indicators. The findings for miR-193b-5p were validated using qRT-PCR in a larger patient cohort, enhancing reliability. In contrast, miR-511-5p showed poor predictive performance and no significant correlations with immunity/inflammation indicators, limiting its utility. A significant limitation for both miR-193b-5p and miR-511-5p is their inability to reliably differentiate between sepsis and septic shock. Challenges include potential generalizability issues due to relatively small initial sample sizes for sequencing, lack of dynamic monitoring throughout disease progression, and conflicting results for miR-193b-5p in previous research. The study underscores the ongoing need for highly specific and sensitive biomarkers, as current clinical markers like CRP, PCT, IL-6, and WBC count lack sufficient speed and accuracy for sepsis diagnosis.
recommended_alternatives: Verifying identified DEMs at cellular and animal levels
Incorporating larger sample sizes for validation in future studies
Dynamic monitoring of biomarker expression throughout disease progression
